Proof 1: Infinitely many primes (Euclid)

Statement: Infinitely many primes (Euclid)

Hypotheses: None

Conclusion: there are infinitely many primes

Definitions: prime, infinitely many

Proof (Variation #1):

Step 1: Assume finitely many primes p_1,...,p_n

Step 2: Define N = p_1 * p_2 * ... * p_n + 1

Step 3: N > 1, so N has a prime factor p

Step 4: If p = p_i for some i, then p divides N and p_i divides N

Step 5: But p_i cannot divide N - p_1*...*p_n = 1, contradiction

Step 6: So p is a new prime not in the list

ID: 9e0bf9dcc93e | Status: UNFORMALIZED | Complexity: O(n)

Mutation test: No removable hypothesis - self-contained

Provenance: Variation #1 for theorem in domain Number_Theory

Proof 2: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Statement: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Hypotheses: p prime, a integer, gcd(a,p) = 1

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #2):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

ID: d47520e4d743 | Status: UNFORMALIZED | Complexity: O(n^2)

Mutation test: Removing 'gcd(a,p)=1': 2^3 = 8 = 0 mod 4, not 1

Provenance: Variation #2 for theorem in domain Number_Theory

Proof 3: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #3):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

ID: f90222721ee2 | Status: UNFORMALIZED | Complexity: O(n log n)

Mutation test: Removing 'p prime': 3! = 6 = 2 mod 4, not -1

Provenance: Variation #3 for theorem in domain Number_Theory

Proof 4: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Statement: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Hypotheses: n_1,...,n_k pairwise coprime, a_1,...,a_k integers

Conclusion: exists unique x mod N=n_1*...*n_k with x = a_i mod n_i

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #4):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

ID: 77a8f203388b | Status: UNFORMALIZED | Complexity: O(1)

Mutation test: Removing coprimality: x=0 mod 2, x=1 mod 4 has no solution

Provenance: Variation #4 for theorem in domain Number_Theory

Proof 5: Dirichlet: if gcd(a,d)=1, infinitely many primes ≡ a mod d

Statement: Dirichlet: if gcd(a,d)=1, infinitely many primes ≡ a mod d

Hypotheses: d >= 1, gcd(a,d) = 1

Conclusion: infinitely many primes p ≡ a (mod d)

Definitions: Dirichlet, primes, arithmetic progression

Proof (Variation #5):

Step 1: Construct Dirichlet L-function L(s,chi) for characters mod d

Step 2: Show L(1,chi) != 0 for all chi

Step 3: Connect to sum 1/p over primes in AP

Step 4: If finite, L-function would have pole or zero at s=1

Step 5: Both contradict established properties

ID: 98c8885af682 | Status: UNFORMALIZED | Complexity: O(n^3)

Mutation test: Removing 'gcd(a,d)=1': 2,4,6,... has only one prime (2)

Provenance: Variation #5 for theorem in domain Number_Theory

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Statement: Dirichlet: if gcd(a,d)=1, infinitely many primes ≡ a mod d

Hypotheses: d >= 1, gcd(a,d) = 1

Conclusion: infinitely many primes p ≡ a (mod d)

Definitions: Dirichlet, primes, arithmetic progression

Proof (Variation #80):

Step 1: Construct Dirichlet L-function L(s,chi) for characters mod d

Step 2: Show L(1,chi) != 0 for all chi

Step 3: Connect to sum 1/p over primes in AP

Step 4: If finite, L-function would have pole or zero at s=1

Step 5: Both contradict established properties

Mutation test: Removing 'gcd(a,d)=1': 2,4,6,... has only one prime (2)

Proof 81: Infinitely many primes (Euclid)

Statement: Infinitely many primes (Euclid)

Hypotheses: None

Conclusion: there are infinitely many primes

Definitions: prime, infinitely many

Proof (Variation #81):

Step 1: Assume finitely many primes p_1,...,p_n

Step 2: Define N = p_1 * p_2 * ... * p_n + 1

Step 3: N > 1, so N has a prime factor p

Step 4: If p = p_i for some i, then p divides N and p_i divides N

Step 5: But p_i cannot divide N - p_1*...*p_n = 1, contradiction

Step 6: So p is a new prime not in the list

ID: e9ca5845ad01 | Status: UNFORMALIZED | Complexity: O(n)

Mutation test: No removable hypothesis - self-contained

Provenance: Variation #81 for theorem in domain Number_Theory

Proof 82: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Statement: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Hypotheses: p prime, a integer, gcd(a,p) = 1

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #82):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

ID: 7d98c6c2bd62 | Status: UNFORMALIZED | Complexity: O(n^2)

Mutation test: Removing 'gcd(a,p)=1': 2^3 = 8 = 0 mod 4, not 1

Provenance: Variation #82 for theorem in domain Number_Theory

Proof 83: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #83):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

ID: 69cdd46777f8 | Status: UNFORMALIZED | Complexity: O(n log n)

Mutation test: Removing 'p prime': 3! = 6 = 2 mod 4, not -1

Provenance: Variation #83 for theorem in domain Number_Theory

Proof 84: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Statement: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Hypotheses: n_1,...,n_k pairwise coprime, a_1,...,a_k integers

Conclusion: exists unique x mod N=n_1*...*n_k with x = a_i mod n_i

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #84):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

ID: ee4727b683c1 | Status: UNFORMALIZED | Complexity: O(1)

Mutation test: Removing coprimality: x=0 mod 2, x=1 mod 4 has no solution

Provenance: Variation #84 for theorem in domain Number_Theory

Proof 107: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Statement: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Hypotheses: p prime, a integer, gcd(a,p) = 1

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #107):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Proof 108: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #108):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Proof 109: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Statement: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Hypotheses: n_1,...,n_k pairwise coprime, a_1,...,a_k integers

Conclusion: exists unique x mod N=n_1*...*n_k with x = a_i mod n_i

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #109):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #188):

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Proof 213: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #213):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #214):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #217):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Statement: Infinitely many primes (Euclid)

Hypotheses: None

Conclusion: there are infinitely many primes

Definitions: prime, infinitely many

Proof (Variation #266):

Step 1: Assume finitely many primes p_1,...,p_n

Step 2: Define N = p_1 * p_2 * ... * p_n + 1

Step 3: N > 1, so N has a prime factor p

Step 4: If p = p_i for some i, then p divides N and p_i divides N

Step 5: But p_i cannot divide N - p_1*...*p_n = 1, contradiction

Step 6: So p is a new prime not in the list

Proof 267: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Statement: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Hypotheses: p prime, a integer, gcd(a,p) = 1

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #267):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

ID: b11e4292156f | Status: UNFORMALIZED | Complexity: O(n^2)

Mutation test: Removing 'gcd(a,p)=1': 2^3 = 8 = 0 mod 4, not 1

Provenance: Variation #267 for theorem in domain Number_Theory

Proof 268: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #268):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Provenance: Variation #268 for theorem in domain Number_Theory

Proof 269: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Statement: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Hypotheses: n_1,...,n_k pairwise coprime, a_1,...,a_k integers

Conclusion: exists unique x mod N=n_1*...*n_k with x = a_i mod n_i

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #269):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Mutation test: Removing coprimality: x=0 mod 2, x=1 mod 4 has no solution

Hypotheses: n_1,...,n_k pairwise coprime, a_1,...,a_k integers

Conclusion: exists unique x mod N=n_1*...*n_k with x = a_i mod n_i

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #319):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Step 3: N > 1, so N has a prime factor p

Step 4: If p = p_i for some i, then p divides N and p_i divides N

Step 5: But p_i cannot divide N - p_1*...*p_n = 1, contradiction

Step 6: So p is a new prime not in the list

Proof 322: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Statement: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Hypotheses: p prime, a integer, gcd(a,p) = 1

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #322):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Mutation test: Removing 'gcd(a,p)=1': 2^3 = 8 = 0 mod 4, not 1

Proof 323: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #323):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Proof (Variation #348):

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Hypotheses: d >= 1, gcd(a,d) = 1

Conclusion: infinitely many primes p ≡ a (mod d)

Definitions: Dirichlet, primes, arithmetic progression

Proof (Variation #425):

Step 1: Construct Dirichlet L-function L(s,chi) for characters mod d

Step 2: Show L(1,chi) != 0 for all chi

Step 3: Connect to sum 1/p over primes in AP

Step 4: If finite, L-function would have pole or zero at s=1

Step 5: Both contradict established properties

Mutation test: Removing 'gcd(a,d)=1': 2,4,6,... has only one prime (2)

Proof 426: Infinitely many primes (Euclid)

Statement: Infinitely many primes (Euclid)

Hypotheses: None

Conclusion: there are infinitely many primes

Definitions: prime, infinitely many

Proof (Variation #426):

Step 1: Assume finitely many primes p_1,...,p_n

Step 2: Define N = p_1 * p_2 * ... * p_n + 1

Step 3: N > 1, so N has a prime factor p

Step 4: If p = p_i for some i, then p divides N and p_i divides N

Step 5: But p_i cannot divide N - p_1*...*p_n = 1, contradiction

Step 6: So p is a new prime not in the list

Proof 427: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Statement: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Hypotheses: p prime, a integer, gcd(a,p) = 1

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #427):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Mutation test: Removing 'gcd(a,p)=1': 2^3 = 8 = 0 mod 4, not 1

Provenance: Variation #427 for theorem in domain Number_Theory

Proof 428: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #428):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Provenance: Variation #428 for theorem in domain Number_Theory

Proof 429: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Statement: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Hypotheses: n_1,...,n_k pairwise coprime, a_1,...,a_k integers

Conclusion: exists unique x mod N=n_1*...*n_k with x = a_i mod n_i

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #429):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Statement: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Hypotheses: p prime, a integer, gcd(a,p) = 1

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #452):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Mutation test: Removing 'gcd(a,p)=1': 2^3 = 8 = 0 mod 4, not 1

Provenance: Variation #452 for theorem in domain Number_Theory

Proof 453: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #453):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Proof 454: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Statement: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Hypotheses: n_1,...,n_k pairwise coprime, a_1,...,a_k integers

Conclusion: exists unique x mod N=n_1*...*n_k with x = a_i mod n_i

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #454):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Mutation test: Removing coprimality: x=0 mod 2, x=1 mod 4 has no solution

Proof 455: Dirichlet: if gcd(a,d)=1, infinitely many primes ≡ a mod d

Hypotheses: d >= 1, gcd(a,d) = 1

Conclusion: infinitely many primes p ≡ a (mod d)

Definitions: Dirichlet, primes, arithmetic progression

Proof (Variation #455):

Step 1: Construct Dirichlet L-function L(s,chi) for characters mod d

Step 2: Show L(1,chi) != 0 for all chi

Step 3: Connect to sum 1/p over primes in AP

Step 4: If finite, L-function would have pole or zero at s=1

Step 5: Both contradict established properties

Proof 456: Infinitely many primes (Euclid)

Statement: Infinitely many primes (Euclid)

Hypotheses: None

Conclusion: there are infinitely many primes

Definitions: prime, infinitely many

Proof (Variation #456):

Step 1: Assume finitely many primes p_1,...,p_n

Step 2: Define N = p_1 * p_2 * ... * p_n + 1

Step 3: N > 1, so N has a prime factor p

Step 4: If p = p_i for some i, then p divides N and p_i divides N

Step 5: But p_i cannot divide N - p_1*...*p_n = 1, contradiction

Step 6: So p is a new prime not in the list

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Proof 558: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #558):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Proof 559: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Hypotheses: n_1,...,n_k pairwise coprime, a_1,...,a_k integers

Conclusion: exists unique x mod N=n_1*...*n_k with x = a_i mod n_i

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #559):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Statement: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Hypotheses: p prime, a integer, gcd(a,p) = 1

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #562):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Proof 587: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #587):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Proof 588: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #588):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Proof 612: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Statement: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Hypotheses: p prime, a integer, gcd(a,p) = 1

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #612):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Proof 613: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #613):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Proof 614: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Hypotheses: n_1,...,n_k pairwise coprime, a_1,...,a_k integers

Conclusion: exists unique x mod N=n_1*...*n_k with x = a_i mod n_i

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #614):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #638):

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Proof 664: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Statement: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Hypotheses: n_1,...,n_k pairwise coprime, a_1,...,a_k integers

Conclusion: exists unique x mod N=n_1*...*n_k with x = a_i mod n_i

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #664):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Hypotheses: None

Conclusion: there are infinitely many primes

Proof (Variation #666):

Step 4: If p = p_i for some i, then p divides N and p_i divides N

Step 5: But p_i cannot divide N - p_1*...*p_n = 1, contradiction

Step 6: So p is a new prime not in the list

Proof 667: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Statement: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Hypotheses: p prime, a integer, gcd(a,p) = 1

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #667):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Proof 668: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #668):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Statement: Infinitely many primes (Euclid)

Hypotheses: None

Conclusion: there are infinitely many primes

Proof (Variation #691):

Step 1: Assume finitely many primes p_1,...,p_n

Step 2: Define N = p_1 * p_2 * ... * p_n + 1

Step 3: N > 1, so N has a prime factor p

Step 4: If p = p_i for some i, then p divides N and p_i divides N

Step 5: But p_i cannot divide N - p_1*...*p_n = 1, contradiction

Step 6: So p is a new prime not in the list

Proof 692: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Statement: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Hypotheses: p prime, a integer, gcd(a,p) = 1

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #692):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Proof 693: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #693):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Proof 694: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Statement: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Hypotheses: n_1,...,n_k pairwise coprime, a_1,...,a_k integers

Conclusion: exists unique x mod N=n_1*...*n_k with x = a_i mod n_i

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #694):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Proof 717: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Statement: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Hypotheses: p prime, a integer, gcd(a,p) = 1

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #717):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Proof 718: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #718):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Proof 719: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Statement: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Hypotheses: n_1,...,n_k pairwise coprime, a_1,...,a_k integers

Conclusion: exists unique x mod N=n_1*...*n_k with x = a_i mod n_i

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #719):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #743):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Proof 744: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Statement: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Hypotheses: n_1,...,n_k pairwise coprime, a_1,...,a_k integers

Conclusion: exists unique x mod N=n_1*...*n_k with x = a_i mod n_i

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #744):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Step 3: N > 1, so N has a prime factor p

Step 4: If p = p_i for some i, then p divides N and p_i divides N

Step 5: But p_i cannot divide N - p_1*...*p_n = 1, contradiction

Step 6: So p is a new prime not in the list

Statement: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Hypotheses: p prime, a integer, gcd(a,p) = 1

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #747):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Proof 797: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Statement: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Hypotheses: p prime, a integer, gcd(a,p) = 1

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #797):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Proof 798: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #798):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Proof 799: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Statement: Chinese Remainder Theorem: system x = a_i mod n_i solvable for coprime n_i

Hypotheses: n_1,...,n_k pairwise coprime, a_1,...,a_k integers

Conclusion: exists unique x mod N=n_1*...*n_k with x = a_i mod n_i

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #799):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #877):

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Proof 878: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Proof (Variation #878):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Proof 928: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #928):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Hypotheses: n_1,...,n_k pairwise coprime, a_1,...,a_k integers

Conclusion: exists unique x mod N=n_1*...*n_k with x = a_i mod n_i

Definitions: CRT, modular, coprime

Proof (Variation #954):

Step 1: For each i, let N_i = N/n_i

Step 2: Since gcd(n_i, N_i) = 1, find s_i with N_i*s_i = 1 (mod n_i)

Step 3: Set x = sum a_i * N_i * s_i

Step 4: Check: x mod n_j = a_j * N_j * s_j = a_j (mod n_j)

Step 5: Uniqueness: if x' also works, x-x' = 0 mod n_i for all i

Step 6: Since n_i coprime, N | (x-x')

Proof 955: Dirichlet: if gcd(a,d)=1, infinitely many primes ≡ a mod d

Statement: Dirichlet: if gcd(a,d)=1, infinitely many primes ≡ a mod d

Hypotheses: d >= 1, gcd(a,d) = 1

Conclusion: infinitely many primes p ≡ a (mod d)

Definitions: Dirichlet, primes, arithmetic progression

Proof (Variation #955):

Step 1: Construct Dirichlet L-function L(s,chi) for characters mod d

Step 2: Show L(1,chi) != 0 for all chi

Step 3: Connect to sum 1/p over primes in AP

Step 4: If finite, L-function would have pole or zero at s=1

Step 5: Both contradict established properties

Proof 956: Infinitely many primes (Euclid)

Statement: Infinitely many primes (Euclid)

Hypotheses: None

Conclusion: there are infinitely many primes

Definitions: prime, infinitely many

Proof (Variation #956):

Step 1: Assume finitely many primes p_1,...,p_n

Step 2: Define N = p_1 * p_2 * ... * p_n + 1

Step 3: N > 1, so N has a prime factor p

Step 4: If p = p_i for some i, then p divides N and p_i divides N

Step 5: But p_i cannot divide N - p_1*...*p_n = 1, contradiction

Step 6: So p is a new prime not in the list

Proof 957: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Statement: Fermat's little theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p for gcd(a,p)=1

Hypotheses: p prime, a integer, gcd(a,p) = 1

Conclusion: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Definitions: Fermat, modular arithmetic, prime

Proof (Variation #957):

Step 1: Consider the set {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p

Step 2: Claim: these are all distinct mod p

Step 3: If ia = ja (mod p), then p | a(i-j), so p | (i-j) since gcd(a,p)=1

Step 4: But 1 <= i,j <= p-1, so 0 < |i-j| < p, contradiction

Step 5: The set is a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}

Step 6: Multiply: a^(p-1) * (p-1)! = (p-1)! (mod p)

Step 7: Cancel (p-1)!: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p)

Mutation test: Removing 'gcd(a,p)=1': 2^3 = 8 = 0 mod 4, not 1

Proof 958: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Statement: Wilson's theorem: (p-1)! = -1 mod p iff p is prime

Hypotheses: p prime

Conclusion: (p-1)! = -1 (mod p)

Definitions: Wilson, factorial, modular

Proof (Variation #958):

Step 1: For each a in {1,...,p-1}, there exists unique a^{-1} in {1,...,p-1}

Step 2: a = a^{-1} iff a^2 = 1 (mod p) iff a = 1 or a = p-1

Step 3: Pair up the remaining p-3 elements into (p-3)/2 pairs

Step 4: Each pair contributes 1 to the product

Step 5: Total product = 1 * (p-1) * 1^{(p-3)/2} = p-1 = -1 (mod p)
